title: Turned from Idols to Serve the Living God
summary: Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy greet the church in Thessalonica and thank God for their work of faith, labor of love, and enduring hope. They recall how the gospel came to the city with power and the Holy Spirit, and how the Thessalonians welcomed it with joy in spite of suffering. News of how they turned from idols to serve the living God and to wait for his Son from heaven has spread through Macedonia, Achaia, and beyond.
story: This chapter is a window onto the very first generation of Christians and very likely the earliest of Paul's letters to survive. A few months earlier Paul and his companions had arrived in Thessalonica after being beaten and jailed in Philippi, preached for some weeks, gathered a church, and then been driven out by a riot (Acts 17:1-10). Paul had worried that the young believers would give up under pressure. Timothy has just brought word that they have not (3:6), and this chapter overflows with thanks. It also summarizes the whole Christian message in its earliest written form: God the Father, the Lord Jesus Christ, the Holy Spirit, conversion from idols, and waiting for the risen Son who rescues from the wrath to come.
historical:
Paul wrote from Corinth around AD 50 or 51. Acts 18 records his arrival there and the arrival of Silas and Timothy from Macedonia. An inscription found at Delphi dates the term of Gallio, the proconsul before whom Paul appeared in Corinth (Acts 18:12), to about AD 51 to 52, which is one of the fixed points for dating Paul's life. Silvanus, named first among Paul's companions, is the Latin form of the name Silas, the prophet from the Jerusalem church who traveled with Paul on this trip (Acts 15:22, 40). Timothy had joined them at Lystra (Acts 16:1-3).

Thessalonica was the capital of the Roman province of Macedonia, a busy port on the Via Egnatia, the main Roman road across the Balkans. That location helps explain verse 8: news from Thessalonica traveled quickly, along with merchants and travelers, to Macedonia and to Achaia (southern Greece, with its capital at Corinth). Acts describes converts from the synagogue, including God-fearing Greeks (Gentiles who worshiped Israel's God without becoming Jews), but verse 9 suggests that many members came straight from pagan worship.
cultural:
To turn from idols meant far more than a private change of belief. Religion in a Greek city was woven into everything: family meals honored household gods, trade guilds held feasts in honor of patron deities, and civic life included festivals and honors for the gods and for Rome and its emperors. Thessalonica had temples and cults to many gods, including Egyptian gods, Dionysus, and the local cult of Cabirus. A person who stopped honoring the gods could be seen as disloyal to family and city, and even as a danger, since the gods were thought to protect the community. That is part of why the Thessalonians suffered for their faith (verse 6; 2:14).

The Jewish Scriptures called Israel's God the living and true God in contrast to idols, which have mouths but cannot speak (Psalm 115; Jeremiah 10). Paul uses that language for Gentiles who have come to worship Israel's God. The phrase the coming wrath also comes from the prophets' warnings of God's judgment on the Day of the Lord.
literary: The chapter follows the pattern of an ancient letter: senders, recipients, greeting, and then a thanksgiving. In Paul's letters the thanksgiving usually introduces the letter's main concerns, and here it is especially long; some scholars think it extends through 3:13. It is one long outpouring in Greek, beginning in verse 2 and running to the end of the chapter. At its heart is the triad of faith, love, and hope (verse 3), which Paul will return to in 5:8. The chapter moves outward in rings: from Paul's prayers, to God's choice of the church, to the church's welcome of the message, to its reputation in Macedonia and Achaia and every place. Verses 9 and 10 are so compact that many scholars think they echo a summary of early missionary preaching to Gentiles.

outline.t: Thanks for faith, love, and hope
Chosen by God: the gospel came in power
From idols to the living God, awaiting his Son

doctrines.note: In a few verses Paul speaks of God the Father, the Lord Jesus Christ as God's Son, and the Holy Spirit, who gave power to the preaching and joy to the hearers (verses 1, 5, 6, and 10). The later doctrine of the Trinity is not spelled out here, but its pattern is present in the earliest Christian letter.

Conversion is described as turning to God from idols, serving him, and waiting for his Son (verses 9 and 10). Salvation includes rescue from the coming wrath through Jesus, whom God raised from the dead. It begins with God's choice (verse 4) and shows itself in faith, love, and hope.

The first mark of the Thessalonians' faith was that they turned from idols. The living and true God cannot share his place with other gods. Turning from idols was costly in their world and remains the necessary other side of turning to God.

words.note: Epistrepho, to turn or turn back. The word describes conversion as a change of direction: away from idols and toward God. It echoes the Old Testament prophets' call for Israel to turn (or return) to the Lord. Faith in this chapter is not only agreement with ideas but a reoriented life.

Ekloge, choosing or election. Paul says he knows God has chosen the Thessalonians, and the evidence he gives is how the gospel came to them with power and how they received it (verses 4 to 6). Election here is not a subject for speculation but a reason for confidence and thanks, known by its fruit.

Anameno, to wait for or await, used only here in the New Testament. It describes expectant waiting for someone who is certain to come. The Thessalonians' faith has a forward lean: they serve God now while waiting for his Son from heaven.

christ: The chapter's final verse is a miniature creed. Jesus is God's Son, now in heaven, whom God raised from the dead, who is coming again, and who is our deliverer from the coming wrath (verse 10). He is also named alongside God the Father as the source of grace and peace (verse 1), which places him with God rather than among creatures. The Thessalonians became imitators of the Lord (verse 6) by receiving the word with joy in suffering, just as Jesus himself endured suffering. Twenty years after the cross, in a letter to Gentile converts, the risen and returning Jesus is already the center of Christian faith and hope.
questions: Paul thanks God for their work of faith, labor of love, and enduring hope. Which of the three is most visible in your life, and which is weakest?
What might turning from idols look like for someone today who has never bowed to a statue?
The Thessalonians received the word with joy in the middle of great suffering. How can joy and suffering exist together?
